source.title_on_document: A Novel Idea Generation Tool using a Structured Conversational AI (CAI) System

paper_design_summary: Thirty postgraduate product design students were split at random into six groups of five, and each group got one product design problem. Every participant first generated ideas for 20 minutes with a conventional ideation technique and no computer (Part A), then for 20 minutes with the authors' GPT-based conversational ideation interface (Part B), always in that order. Expert design researchers rated the ideas for novelty and variety on 1 to 5 scales, the authors counted ideas for fluency, and a panel of twenty experts chose the more meaningful idea in six Part A versus Part B pairs.

studies.label: Pilot study (conventional ideation, then CAI-based ideation)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Only the design problem statement was randomized (groups of five to one of six problems). AI use was not randomized: every participant did Part A (conventional techniques, no AI) and then Part B (CAI tool), in a fixed order.
assignment.quote: The participants were randomly divided into six groups, each assigned a specific design problem statement. ... A protocol was designed to conduct the study in two phases for each participating designer.
assignment.locator: p. 8, Section 6 (Pilot Study); p. 9, Section 6.1.3 (Study Design)

arms.name: Part A: conventional ideation
arms.description: Each group used one assigned conventional technique (Brainstorming, Random Words, SCAMPER, Synectics, Analogous Thinking) for 20 minutes, with no computer or digital gadget.

arms.name: Part B: CAI-based ideation
arms.description: The same participants used the GPT-based conversational ideation interface for 20 minutes and shortlisted ideas; the paper says Part B centred on collective refinement and curation of GPT ideas as a group.

participants.exclusions: Thirty students were recruited and the protocol puts each through both parts. The paper gives no count analyzed and reports no exclusions, so at most 30 people were analyzed. AI condition was not randomized, so no count randomized to AI exists.
participants.quote: thirty postgraduate product design students were recruited (Figure 4). The participants were randomly divided into six groups, each assigned a specific design problem statement.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 design chatbot with an adjacent moodboard, built in Unity and C#; described by the authors as a custom fine-tuned GPT model (p. 7, Section 4.4.1 and footnotes 1-2; p. 8, Section 5)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants prompted the GPT design chatbot by text or voice, adjusted its temperature setting, and framed or shortlisted the generated ideas on an adjacent moodboard.

task.description: Generate product ideas for one of six design problem statements (for example waste segregation, footwear cleaning, umbrella drying)

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas generated in 20 minutes)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas per problem statement (one group of five per problem), plotted for six problem statements in Figure 6.

contrasts.reported: the conventional vs CAI-aided ideation produced an average of 4.8 and 15 ideas in 20 minutes, respectively

outcomes.name: Novelty rating of individual ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 1 to 5 Likert ratings by 80 expert respondents (design researchers at IIT Delhi, IIT Guwahati, IIT Bombay, IISc Bangalore) through an online questionnaire; means by problem statement in Figure 7, Part B box plot in Figure 8.

contrasts.reported: the average rating for Part A is 2.5, while Part B is 3.86

outcomes.name: Variety rating of a set of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 1 to 5 Likert variety ratings by 80 experts of a set of twelve ideas randomly picked from about 80. Variety is diversity among ideas within one problem statement (one group), so it is coded flexibility, not across-people diversity. Means by problem statement in Figure 9.

contrasts.reported: the average variety rating for Part A is 2.9, while Part B is 4.2

outcomes.name: Meaningfulness of idea statements (expert pairwise judgments)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Twenty expert product designers chose the more meaningful statement in each of six idea pairs, with one idea from Part A and one from Part B presented in random order. Figure 5(a) reports average voting proportions and Figure 5(b) plots votes for the statements. These are evaluator judgments of the outputs, not counts of students receiving AI assistance. The exact number of analyzed judgments is not stated (p. 10, Section 6.2.1 and Figure 5).

contrasts.reported: 68% of the experts found the ideas produced by the GPT more meaningful. Figure 5(a): CAI Generated 68%; Designer Generated 32%.

outcomes.name: Elaboration (average word count and related linguistic counts)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average word counts of idea statements, with noun, verb, and adjective counts as related measures of linguistic detail. The authors report higher counts for GPT-generated ideas. Figure 10 displays the linguistic categories for GPT and designer ideas in a sunburst chart without numerical values; exact means and the number of analyzed outputs are not stated. The counting method is not described, and no codebook measure category exactly fits raw linguistic counts, so measure is null (pp. 12-13, Section 6.3 and Figure 10).

contrasts.reported: GPT, on average, has a higher count of linguistic elements such as words, nouns, verbs, and adjectives.
contrasts.locator: p. 12, Section 6.3 (last paragraph); p. 13, Figure 10 and continuation of Section 6.3

eligibility.reason: Thirty students took part (p. 8), well below 50. AI use was not randomized: all participants did the no-AI part first and the AI part second, and only the problem statement was assigned at random (pp. 8-9). Expert ratings of novelty and variety are scored on the ideas. This is a small non-randomized before-and-after comparison, not a small randomized experiment.

one_line_finding: In a fixed-order pilot with 30 design students, GPT-aided ideation produced more ideas (15 vs 4.8 in 20 minutes), higher expert novelty ratings (3.86 vs 2.5), and higher variety ratings (4.2 vs 2.9) than conventional ideation, with no test statistics reported (pp. 10 and 12, Figures 6, 7, 9).
